name: Citizenship by Marriage to a Nicaraguan Citizen

requirements.blocker_text: Ley de Nacionalidad (Ley No. 149, 1992): a foreign spouse married to a Nicaraguan citizen may naturalize after 2 years of residence, provided the marital bond still exists at the time of application ('siempre que permanezca el vinculo conyugal') and other general naturalization requirements are met. The law's language is explicitly gender-neutral.
requirements.fix_path: Marry a Nicaraguan citizen, remain married while accumulating 2 years of residence, and apply.

evidence_required.document: Proof of continuous marital bond and residence

outcome.physical_presence_requirement: 2 years, contingent on the marriage remaining intact

sources.title: UNHCR (ACNUR) -- hosted primary legal text of Nicaragua's Ley de Nacionalidad (Ley No. 149, 1992), marriage-based naturalization provision

Divergentes (independent Nicaraguan news outlet) -- Law 1268 (effective 16 Jan 2026), reforming Constitution Articles 23 and 25 to bar dual nationality for naturalizing Nicaraguans, except Central Americans by origin

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Nicaragua). STATUS: DRAFT -- the residence/marriage-duration requirement is sourced to a UNHCR-hosted 1992 statutory text, tier 2; the current dual-nationality consequence is sourced only to an independent news outlet, tier 4 (a government or Official Gazette confirmation of Law 1268's exact text was not independently fetched in this build). MAJOR, CURRENT, WELL-DOCUMENTED FINDING, FLAGGED PROMINENTLY: as of 16 January 2026, Nicaragua became the only Central American country to bar dual nationality outright for people who naturalize -- a foreign spouse acquiring Nicaraguan citizenship through THIS route must now renounce their original nationality permanently (the reform is prospective, not retroactive), UNLESS they are a Central American national by origin, who retains a preserved exception. dual_citizenship_allowed set false accordingly for this route (non-Central-American spouses) -- this is a genuine, recent reversal from the 1992 law's more flexible reciprocity-based framework, and a rare case in this dataset (alongside Burkina Faso's marriage-citizenship tightening) of a country's citizenship regime becoming MORE restrictive rather than more open.
